ENGL.description: A study of dramatic texts and traditions, offering attention to major dramatic modes and movements such as Ritual, Dance, Naturalism, Expressionism, Absurdism, Political Theatre, Feminist Theatre, and Global/Intercultural Theatre. Each will be investigated in the context of performance videos, live performances, and/or written text.

ENGL.title: American Literatures I
ENGL.description:
Introduction to the traditions of American literature through 1865.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2702 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: American Literatures II
ENGL.description:
Introduction to the traditions of American literature after 1865.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2702 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Indigenous Drama
ENGL.description:
A study of dramatic literatures and theatre practice from Indigenous theatre makers, including playwrights, directors, and other practitioners.
Also listed as INDG 2709.

ENGL.title: Culture and Climate Change
ENGL.description: Selected topics related to climate change and cultural studies.

ENGL.title: Indigenous and Canadian Literatures
ENGL.description: A survey of  Canadian literary cultures in English from their beginnings to the present that frames them in the wider context of Indigenous writing and storytelling. This course is writing-attentive.

ENGL.title: Literature of the Self
ENGL.description: A study of developments in the literary representation of the self. The course considers a wide range of major texts from the Middle Ages to the present.

ENGL.title: Writing Poetry
ENGL.description: A workshop involving regular assignments in writing poetry and practical criticism based on this work. Permission to register in this course  requires the student to submit a writing sample. Instructions can be found at carleton.ca/english.

ENGL.title: Writing Fiction
ENGL.description: A workshop involving regular assignments in writing prose fiction and practical criticism based on this work. Permission to register in this course  requires the student to submit a writing sample. Instructions can be found at carleton.ca/english.

ENGL.title: Culture and Society
ENGL.description: A study of literature in relation to its social and political contexts. Topics and periods vary.

ENGL.title: Celtic Literatures
ENGL.description:
The literatures of Ireland, Scotland, and/or Wales. Topics will vary in national and historical scope and may be organized by theme, author, and/or genre.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2602 and ENGL 2606 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Book Arts Workshop
ENGL.description: This experiential learning course immerses students in the practical arts and histories of book production.

ENGL.title: Writing Creative Nonfiction
ENGL.description: A workshop involving regular assignments in reading and writing creative nonfiction and practical criticism based on this work.  Permission to register in this course requires the student to submit a writing sample.  Instructions can be found at carleton.ca/english.

ENGL.title: Topics in Decolonization and Migration I
ENGL.description: An introduction to the study of literature and culture in the context of topics such as empire and decolonization, diaspora, migration and globalization, race, and ethnicity. Themes, authors, and geographical and temporal focus will vary.

ENGL.title: African Literatures I
ENGL.description: An introductory survey of modern African literatures, discourses, and cultural production in the first half of the 20th century.

ENGL.title: African Literatures II
ENGL.description: A survey of modern African literatures, discourses, and cultural production from the era of political independence from colonialism (the 1960s) to the present.

ENGL.title: South Asian Literatures I
ENGL.description:
An introductory historical survey of the literatures of South Asia to the early colonial era, starting with the Indian epics and concluding with literary traditions of 18th-century India.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2502 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: South Asian Literatures II
ENGL.description:
An introductory survey of literatures of South Asia from the colonial and postcolonial eras.  Topics include the nationalist movement, neo-colonialism, and post-colonialism.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2502 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Literatures of the Americas I
ENGL.description:
Introduction to comparative and transnational approaches to the literatures and oratures of the Caribbean, and North and South America, with emphasis on the pre-colonial and colonial eras.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2909 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Literatures of the Americas II
ENGL.description:
Introduction to comparative and transnational approaches to 20th- and 21st-century writing from the Caribbean, and North and South America.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 2909 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Literatures in Translation
ENGL.description: A study of non-English literatures in translation with a special focus on cultural and historical contexts.

ENGL.title: Reading Poetry
ENGL.description: This course is designed to enable students to develop skills in reading and writing about poetry. Readings will be chosen from a variety of authors, periods, and/or genres.

ENGL.title: Studies in Greek Literature
ENGL.description:
A study of an author or topic in Greek literature. Contents of this course vary from year to year.
Also listed as CLCV 3701.

ENGL.title: Studies in Roman Literature
ENGL.description:
A study of an author or topic in Roman literature.
Also listed as CLCV 3702.

ENGL.title: The Secret Lives of Poems
ENGL.description: This course is designed to enable students to develop skills in reading and writing about great works of poetry. Course requirements will feature a combination of creative and critical exercises, but no formal essay.

ENGL.title: Comics and Graphic Novels
ENGL.description: An introduction to the critical study of comic books and graphic narrative.

ENGL.title: Europe, Russia, and Eurasia Beyond Borders: Literature and Culture
ENGL.description:
An exploration of the cultural borders and boundaries of contemporary Europe, Russia, and Eurasia. Using literary and visual texts, the course explores issues such as migration, cultural and political borders and their transcendence, cultural responses to authoritarianism, the Cold War and its afterlives, and memory.
Also listed as EURR 3010.
ENGL.schedule: Lecture and discussion three hours a week

ENGL.title: History of Literary Theory
ENGL.description:
Introduction to ideas about literature, aesthetics, authorship, and readership as these have circulated in periods before the twentieth century.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3000 (no longer offered), and ENGL 3001 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Theories and Critical Practices
ENGL.description: This course offers students an interdisciplinary foundation in cultural, critical, and literary theories and practices.  This course is writing attentive.

ENGL.title: Topics in Medieval Literature
ENGL.description: A study of selected topics and texts from medieval literature.

ENGL.title: European Literature
ENGL.description:
Major movements and works from Dante's Divine Comedy through Voltaire's Candide. Themes include the New Humanism vs. old Chivalry in the Renaissance and Baroque periods; the rise of the modern novel and drama; reason, nature, and the Enlightenment project.
Also listed as HUMS 3200.

ENGL.title: Chaucer
ENGL.description: A study of Chaucer's works including some attention to the Middle English language in which he wrote.

ENGL.title: Literary Representations of Childhood and Youth
ENGL.description:
An examination of the ways in which childhood, children, and youth have been represented in creative literature (fiction, poetry, drama, and/or creative nonfiction).
Also listed as CHST 3204.

ENGL.title: Shakespeare and the Stage
ENGL.description:
Introduction to the study of early modern play-texts written by Shakespeare and/or his contemporaries.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3304 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Shakespeare and Film
ENGL.description: A study of film adaptations of selected plays by Shakespeare.

ENGL.title: The Book in the Digital Age
ENGL.description:
A multidisciplinary course focused on the social, economic and political dimensions of the book in its manuscript, print and digital forms.
Also listed as DIGH 3001.

ENGL.title: 18th-Century Literature
ENGL.description: A detailed study of authors and movements of the period 1660 to 1780.

ENGL.title: Introduction to Professional Writing and Editing
ENGL.description: The fundamental skills of professional writing and editing, including writing for specific audiences, document design, revision strategies, copyediting.

ENGL.title: Professional Writing Practicum
ENGL.description: Experiential learning in Professional Writing via field placement. Students pursue personalized learning outcomes in a workplace practicum. The submission of an application is required.

ENGL.title: Literatures and Cultures 1700-1900
ENGL.description:
A study of the period between 1700 and 1900, with attention to cultural, historical, geographical, and literary contexts.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3502 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Literatures and Cultures 1900-Now
ENGL.description:
A study of the period between 1900 and the present, with attention to cultural, historical, geographical, and literary contexts.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3502 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: The 19th-Century Novel
ENGL.description:
A study of the English novel in the 19 th  century.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3503 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: 20th- and 21st-Century Poetry
ENGL.description: A study of 20th and 21st-century poetry in English. Topics and authors may vary.

ENGL.title: 20th- and 21st-century Fiction
ENGL.description: A study of 20th- and 21st-century fiction in English. Topics and authors may vary.

ENGL.title: Modern and Contemporary Literary Theory
ENGL.description:
Introduction to contemporary approaches to literary texts, such as formalist, structuralist, deconstructive, psychoanalytic, Marxist, historicist, and feminist. Topics may include: the nature and role of literature, of author and reader, of canons, ideology, gender, sexuality, and race.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3002 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Topics in Theatre Management
ENGL.description: A workshop taught by practitioners in the community that provides students with the knowledge and skills necessary to create, manage, and sustain theatre projects. Topics will vary but may include the development of children’s theatre or the operation of a festival or touring company.

ENGL.title: Drama:  Contemporary Performance
ENGL.description: A study of dramatic texts and performance practices in contemporary professional theatre.  Topics vary according to the season programs of professional theatre in Ottawa.  Students will attend a number of productions, determined by the instructor.  Field trip fees will apply.

ENGL.title: American Culture
ENGL.description:
A study of American writing in its cultural and historical contexts.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3703 (no longer offered).

ENGL.title: Canadian Poetry
ENGL.description: A study of Canadian poetry in its social and political contexts.

ENGL.title: Canadian Fiction
ENGL.description: A study of Canadian fiction in its social and political contexts.

ENGL.title: Writing Screenplays
ENGL.description: An intermediate workshop involving regular assignments in writing for film.

ENGL.title: Writing Fiction (Intermediate)
ENGL.description: An intermediate workshop involving regular assignments in writing prose fiction and practical criticism.

ENGL.title: Intermediate Drama Workshop
ENGL.description: A course dealing with techniques of characterization, principles of ensemble performance, scene analysis for actors and directors, styles of performance.

ENGL.title: Topics in Performance
ENGL.description: A study of selected elements of performance. Topics will vary but may include such areas as the theory and practice of comic timing on stage or movement on stage space.
ENGL.schedule: Lecture and workshop three hours a week

ENGL.title: Writing Popular Fiction
ENGL.description: An intermediate workshop in creative writing that focuses on the development of writing skills specific to the crafting of narratives in such genres as Speculative Fiction, Young Adult Fiction, and Historical Fiction.

ENGL.title: Research and Theory in Academic Writing
ENGL.description: Study of contemporary research and theory (1970s to present) on academic writing in elementary, secondary and post-secondary school, with emphasis on writing in university. Consideration of what academic writing entails, how writing fosters learning, and how instruction can help students develop their writing abilities.

ENGL.title: Research and Theory in Workplace Writing
ENGL.description: Study of contemporary research and theory (1980s to present) in writing in workplace settings. Consideration of how writing is used in accomplishing work, how novices learn to write effectively, and what the implications are for pedagogy.

ENGL.title: From English Degree to Career
ENGL.description: This experiential-learning course prepares students in English for their transition into the workplace. Project-based activities (including readings and research) and guest speakers will teach students to identify, develop, and apply the skills and knowledge gained from a degree in English studies.
ENGL.schedule: Lectures and workshops three hours a week

ENGL.title: Cultural Studies
ENGL.description: This course explores cultural expression across diverse media, theorizing culture as a form of struggle that shapes material conditions, fuels knowledge production, and informs lived experience.

ENGL.title: Special Topics in Writing
ENGL.description: An intermediate workshop that involves regular creative writing assignments and practical criticism based on this work. Topics will vary. Yearly special topics can be found at carleton.ca/english/.

ENGL.title: Spoken Word Poetry Workshop
ENGL.description: This intermediate-level workshop-based course explores traditions of spoken word poetry while requiring students to create and perform their own spoken word poems.

ENGL.title: Literary Ecological Fieldwork
ENGL.description: This interdisciplinary, experiential fieldwork course brings together literature, culture, and ecology studies. At least 50% of class periods will be devoted to short field work excursions in the Ottawa region. These excursions will be complemented by classroom discussion time. Field trip fees will apply.

ENGL.title: Topics in Decolonization and Migration II
ENGL.description: An intermediate study of literature, culture, and research in the context of topics such as empire and decolonization, diaspora, migration and globalization, race, and ethnicity. Themes, authors, and geographical and temporal focus will vary.

ENGL.title: Studies in Diaspora Lit.
ENGL.description: A study of diaspora literatures and cultures.

ENGL.title: Studies in Indigenous Literature
ENGL.description: A study of Indigenous literatures and cultures.

ENGL.title: Intro to Postcolonial Theory
ENGL.description: A survey of major concepts and key figures in postcolonial theory.

ENGL.title: Studies in Postcolonial Literature
ENGL.description: A study of postcolonial literatures and cultures. Topics may vary from year to year.

ENGL.title: Studies in Poetry
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in poetry.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in the Novel
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in the novel.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Writing and Knowledge-Making in the Professions
ENGL.description: The role of writing in constructing knowledge in the professions, as viewed from contemporary socio-cultural perspectives.  Consideration of how the goals, values, and assumptions of different professions shape their writing in distinctive ways and what implications this holds for theory, research, and practice.

ENGL.title: Studies in Literary Theory
ENGL.description:
Study of a selected topic in literary theory and criticism.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4000 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Old English
ENGL.description:
Studies in Old English literature and its cultural and historical contexts. Instruction in grammar to facilitate reading knowledge of the Old English language.
Also listed as LING 4805.Precludes additional credit for ENGL 3102 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Culture and the Text
ENGL.description: Topics will vary from year to year.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Digital Culture and the Text I
ENGL.description:
A study of new developments in digital media and culture, and how they affect our understanding of literary modes, genres and textuality, including notions of authorship and reading strategies.  Topics will vary from year to year.
Also listed as DIGH 4002.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Publishing
ENGL.description: Topics will vary from year to year.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Editing a Literary Magazine
ENGL.description: In this experiential learning course students will work collaboratively to design, edit, produce, and publicize issues of a Carleton University literary magazine in digital and/or print formats.

ENGL.title: Digital Culture and the Text II
ENGL.description:
A study of new developments in digital media and culture, and how they affect our understanding of literary modes, genres and textuality, including notions of authorship and reading strategies.  Topics will vary from year to year.
Also listed as DIGH 4003.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Digital Humanities
ENGL.description:
A study of current issues and debates in the Digital Humanities.
Also listed as DIGH 4001.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Medieval Literature
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in Medieval literature; requires previous experience reading medieval English.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Renaissance Literature
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in Renaissance literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in 18th-Century Literature
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in Restoration or 18th-century literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Digital Humanities Workshop
ENGL.description: This workshop will provide students with the opportunity to complete an individual or collaborative capstone project in the Digital Humanities.

ENGL.title: Digital Humanities Practicum
ENGL.description: Practical experience gained by working on projects under the supervision of the staff of a participating public- or private-sector institution or organization, including a final written assignment or equivalent project. A maximum of 1.0 practicum credit may be applied towards degree requirements.

ENGL.title: Studies in Romanticism
ENGL.description:
A study of a selected topic, 1770-1830.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4407 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Teaching Writing in School and the Workplace
ENGL.description: Introduction to approaches for teaching writing in elementary and secondary school, in university, and in the workplace, with a focus on socio-cultural theories of language and learning. Discussion of applications of these approaches to classroom and workplace teaching.

ENGL.title: Studies in Victorian Literature
ENGL.description:
A study of a selected topic in 19th-century British literature, 1830-1900.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4501 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: The Great Russian Novel
ENGL.description:
A study of masterpieces of the Russian tradition, to be selected from among works by writers such as Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Gogol, Turgenev, Bely, Bulgakov, and Nabokov. All novels will be read in English translation.
Also listed as EURR 4103.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Contemporary Poetry
ENGL.description: A comparative and transnational approach to 20th- and 21st -century poetry.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Theatre Production Seminar
ENGL.description: This course offers students advanced engagement with the theory and application of theatrical crafts and includes participation in a writing, acting, or technical capacity on a class production.

ENGL.title: Studies in 20th- and 21st-century Literature
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in literature of the 20th and 21st century.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Global Stages and Theories
ENGL.description: An advanced study of dramatic texts from transnational, postcolonial, or European contexts. This course will offer sustained attention to specific theatre traditions, theatrical practice, and interpretation of texts. Topics and points of emphasis vary from year to year.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in American Literature I
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in American literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in American Literature II
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in American literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Race, Ethnicity and Canadian Lit.
ENGL.description: A study of Canadian literature that engages with notions of race and ethnicity.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Canadian Literature I
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in Canadian literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Studies in Canadian Literature II
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in Canadian literature.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Independent Study
ENGL.description: Independent research and writing, under the supervision of English faculty, requiring an essay of approximately 10,000 words. A written proposal outlining the project must be submitted to the undergraduate supervisor by July 31.

ENGL.title: Writing and Knowledge-Making in the Disciplines
ENGL.description: The role of writing in constructing knowledge in academic disciplines, as viewed from contemporary socio-cultural perspectives. Consideration of how the goals, values, and assumptions of different disciplines shape their writing in distinctive ways and what implications this holds for pedagogy.

ENGL.title: Independent Creative Writing Project
ENGL.description: Independent creative writing, supervised by a Departmental faculty member, resulting in a poetry manuscript (10-15 poems), a one-act play, a 10,000-word novella, or two short stories.  A proposal, coordinated with the faculty supervisor, must be submitted to the Undergraduate Supervisor by July 31.

ENGL.title: Advanced Writing Workshop
ENGL.description: An advanced workshop involving regular assignments in creative writing and practical criticism based on this work.  Topics will vary.

ENGL.title: Issues in Diaspora Literature
ENGL.description:
A study of a selected topic in diaspora literature and culture.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4907 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Topics in Postcolonial and Diaspora Lit. and Theory
ENGL.description: A study of a selected topic in postcolonial and/or diaspora literatures and theories. Themes, authors, and geographical and temporal focus will vary.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Indigenous Literatures I
ENGL.description:
A study of the literatures produced by Indigenous storytellers and writers, with a focus on the oral tradition and life writing.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4808 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Indigenous Literatures II
ENGL.description:
A study of the contemporary period of Indigenous literature, examining the historical and mythic influences on the literature.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4808 and ENGL 4809 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Issues in Postcolonial Theory
ENGL.description: A study of a selected issue in postcolonial and/or diaspora theory.
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENGL.title: Issues in Postcolonial Literature
ENGL.description:
A study of a selected topic in postcolonial literature and culture.
Precludes additional credit for ENGL 4906 (no longer offered).
ENGL.schedule: Seminar or lecture three hours a week

ENSC.title: Environmental Science Seminar
ENSC.description: The purpose and nature of the program; society's view on the natural and human-modified environment; major environmental issues and their scientific aspects; preparation and presentation of paper and seminars.
ENSC.schedule: Lectures, seminars and workshops four hours a week

ENSC.title: Environmental Science Field Methods
ENSC.description: A field-based course introducing students to practical methods in environmental science. Topics will include earth sciences, geography, biology, and chemistry related aspects of environmental sciences and will focus on quantitative techniques to assess environmental impacts and management. A supplementary fee will apply.
ENSC.schedule: lectures and workshops, seven hours per week (delivered on a single day and on up to two mandatory weekend trips)

ENSC.title: Earth Resources and Natural Hazards: Environmental Impacts
ENSC.description: Environmental impact of mineral, energy and water resource exploitation and impact of hazardous Earth processes such as volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and others: their prediction and mitigation.

ENSC.title: Methods and Analysis in Environmental Science
ENSC.description: Study and application of qualitative and quantitative techniques in environmental science, including study design, data collection and assembly, database manipulation, data analysis, and critically evaluating scientific information.
ENSC.schedule: Lectures and seminars three hours a week

ENSC.title: Environmental Science and Management: Theory and Practice
ENSC.description: Theoretical and practical perspectives related to environmental science and management; Emphasis on real-world problems associated with human activities and development of solutions in natural and built environments; Hands-on experience with environmental monitoring and restoration. A supplementary fee will apply.
ENSC.schedule: lectures and workshops, 7 hours per week (delivered on a single day)

ENSC.title: Applied Data Analysis
ENSC.description: Data analysis strategies to tackle real-world, wicked problems. Includes a hands-on applied environmental data science project with a variety of partners. Topics include: obtaining and working with data, exploring causal relationships, data ethics, communicating data, and moving from data to information to action.

ENSC.title: Aquatic Science and Management
ENSC.description: Fundamentals of aquatic science. The physical, chemical, and biotic aspects of lake, river, and estuary systems including human impacts, management and conservation.

ENSC.title: Group Research in Environmental Science
ENSC.description: Major project relating to an issue involving environmental science; effective methods of team research and presentation of group work. May include field work during class time or on weekends.
ENSC.schedule: Lectures, seminars and workshops three hours a week

ENSC.title: Topics in Environmental Science
ENSC.description: Specific topics of current interest.  Topics may vary from year to year.

ENSC.title: Project Planning for Environmental Research
ENSC.description: Independent or group study on the fundamentals of scientific investigation, which may include use of literature, learning of research techniques, and development of a research proposal, in consultation with a Faculty supervisor. May include directed reading, written assignments, tutorials, laboratory or field work.

ENSC.title: Co-operative Work Term
ENSC.description: Practical experience for students enrolled in the Co-operative Option. To receive course credit a student must receive satisfactory evaluations from their work term employer. Written reports describing the work term project will be required. Graded Sat or Uns.

ENSC.title: Environmental Science Practicum
ENSC.description: Experience working in the environmental science sector, applying academic training to practical environmental issues.  Graded Sat/Uns.

ENSC.title: Environmental Decisions
ENSC.description: The regulatory and scientific aspects of environmental management decisions, including risk analysis and mitigation, managing chronic and acute environmental impacts, and conservation of species and landscapes. Students will use real-world case studies to learn traditional and cutting-edge decision-making tools.

ENSC.title: Food Systems and the Environment
ENSC.description: This course explores issues of food systems and their sustainability. We will discuss aspects of food systems, including production, distribution, consumption, waste management, and their impact on communities and the environment.

ENSC.title: Environmental Solutions and Sustainability Science
ENSC.description: Focus on conceptualization and application of different knowledges and knowledge systems to complex, interdisciplinary real-world problems through an environmental lens.  Development of skills and mindset needed to generate creative solutions that will be embraced by diverse publics and decision makers.
ENSC.schedule: Lecture, seminar, or workshops three hours a week

ENSC.title: Topics in Environmental Science
ENSC.schedule: Lectures and discussion three hours a week

ENSC.title: Directed Projects
ENSC.description: Independent or group study, for fourth-year students to explore a particular project, in consultation with a Faculty supervisor. May include directed reading, written assignments, tutorials, laboratory or field work.

ENSC.title: Honours Research Project
ENSC.description: An independent investigation into an aspect of environmental science supervised by a member of the faculty. Approval of the topic and the research schedule must be obtained from the project supervisor and the course coordinator before the last date for registration.

ENSC.title: Translational Approach to Indigenous Community Wellness
ENSC.description: This course involves co-developing an Indigenous community-led process or product that addresses a current and specific mental health issue. Involves working in interdisciplinary groups with a community partner.
ENSC.schedule: Seminars or workshops three hours a week

ENST.title: Introduction to Environmental and Climate Change Studies
ENST.description: A critical introduction to the scholarly field of environmental studies, with an emphasis on society-environment entanglements. It is designed to engage with environmental and climate change issues. Possible themes include population, scarcity, institutions, commons, risks, hazards, markets, political economy, and the social construction of nature.
ENST.schedule: Lecture two hours and workshops/tutorials one hour weekly

ENST.title: People, Places and Environments
ENST.description: Introduction to human geography. Examination of relationships between people, communities, society and the natural environment at local to global scales. Population change, cultural patterns, and historical, economic, political and environmental forces, including climate change,  that shape human activity and experiences from place to place.
ENST.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and tutorial one hour a week

ENST.title: Environmental Justice
ENST.description: Contemporary and foundational theories, practice and praxis of environmental justice in Canadian and comparative settings. Combine and communicate about aspects of the physical, built and social environments to understand how uneven conditions develop. Strategies and ideas to move towards greater equity and good environmental relationships.
ENST.schedule: Lecture two hours a week, discussion one hour a week

ENST.title: Sustainable Futures: Environmental Challenges and Solutions
ENST.description: Individual and collective responses to pressing environmental problems, such as climate change. Innovative ways in which the environment can be protected and restored, taking into consideration socioeconomic, political and cultural factors. Topics include environmental lifestyles, sustainable communities, food systems, environmental design, and political activism.
ENST.schedule: Lectures, seminars and field work three hours a week

ENST.title: Introduction to Qualitative Research
ENST.description: Introduction to the research process, from generating questions through to reporting results. Topics include intensive and extensive research approaches; the use of surveys, interviews and other data collection methods; the analysis of qualitative information; and the ethical dimensions of doing research with people and communities.
ENST.schedule: Lectures two hours a week, workshop two hours a week

ENST.title: Introduction to Quantitative Research
ENST.description: Introduction to solving problems using descriptive and inferential statistical methods. Graphical and numerical tools to describe distributions. Probability, sampling and estimates, and hypothesis testing. Fundamentals of spatial statistics and analysis.
ENST.schedule: Lectures two hours a week, laboratory two hours a week

ENST.title: Climate Change: Social Science Perspectives
ENST.description: An introduction to climate change as a political, economic and socio-cultural phenomenon, including the political-economic and world-historical causes of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions; variations in impact and vulnerability; climate justice and other political movements; global mitigation and adaptation strategies; and proposals for radical systemic change.
ENST.schedule: Lectures two hours a week, discussion groups one hour a week

ENST.title: Nature, Environment and Society
ENST.description: Overview of social science perspectives analyzing the relationship of nature and society.  Examination of environmental problems, responses, and potential solutions through the study of concepts, theories, and research drawn from a range of scholarly approaches to environmental and climate change studies.
ENST.schedule: Lecture and discussion three hours a week

ENST.title: Environmental and Natural Resources
ENST.description: Exploration of complexity, dynamics, uncertainty and equity issues underpinning environmental and resource issues; review and appraisal of selected contemporary methods to assess and manage environmental and natural resources.

ENST.title: Climate Justice and Action: Organizing for a Just, Equitable and Sustainable World
ENST.description: Exploration of how communities and movements fight the climate crisis and build alternative futures. It combines critical theory with hands-on learning to examine the collective actions and organizing strategies through which social movements tackle the systemic factors shaping climate change and its uneven impacts.

ENST.title: Honours Field Course
ENST.description: Field research, with a focus on data collection methods, analysis and presentation of findings. Design and conduct research that links the human and biophysical environment. Topics may change from year to year.

ENST.title: Environmental and Climate Change Studies Seminar
ENST.description: An advanced seminar designed to provide a capstone experience that builds upon and applies the analytical skills and interdisciplinary knowledge acquired in the Environmental Studies program. Topics vary year to year and by course section (see departmental website).

ENST.title: Environmental Studies Practicum I
ENST.description: Students apply their knowledge and research skills and gain experience through field placements in government, the private sector, non-government organisations and with community organisations in the environmental field.

ENST.title: Environmental Studies Practicum II
ENST.description: Students apply their knowledge and research skills and gain experience through field placements in government, the private sector, non-government organisations and with community organisations in the environmental field.

ENST.title: Environmental Impact Assessment
ENST.description: Principles, scope and purpose of environmental impact assessment, from conceptual and methodological points of view; range of environmental issues, with emphasis on Canadian case studies.
ENST.schedule: Lectures and seminars three hours per week

ENST.title: Directed Studies in Environmental Studies
ENST.description: Students pursue their interest in a selected theme in environmental studies on a tutorial basis with a faculty member.

ENST.title: Environmental Policy Analysis
ENST.description: Critical examination of the creation, implementation and effectiveness of government policies related to environmental issues. Emphasis on perspectives, actors, institutions and social and economic relationships affecting policy responses to these issues, and on tools for analyzing the implications of specific policy choices.

ENST.title: Special Topics in Geography and Environmental Studies
ENST.description:
Selected topics in geography and/or environmental studies.
Also listed as GEOG 4007.Precludes additional credit for GEOG 4006 (no longer offered).

ENST.title: Seminar in People, Resources, and Environmental Change
ENST.description:
A selected topic or field of inquiry concerning natural resource use and environmental change.
Also listed as GEOG 4022.

ENST.title: Environmental and Geographic Education
ENST.description:
Selected theoretical and applied issues concerning environmental and geographic education.
Also listed as GEOG 4050.

ENST.title: Field Studies
ENST.description: Field observation and methodology in a selected region, special topic or contemporary problem; on an individual or group basis.

ENST.title: Community-Engaged Research
ENST.description: Working in partnership with local organizations, students apply their geographical knowledge to conduct community-engaged research. Student projects will generate outputs for community partners. Research topics vary year to year.
ENST.schedule: Lectures, discussion and project work three hours a week

ENST.title: Honours Research Project
ENST.description: An independent investigation into a select aspect of environmental studies, supervised by a faculty member. Possible outcomes might include: workshops, audio-visual productions, lay publications, and field projects accompanied by an essay demonstrating the student's capacity to critically reflect on the research project.

ENST.title: Honours Research Essay
ENST.description: Interdisciplinary research essay on an environmental issue, carried out in consultation with a faculty supervisor. The student must consult with the undergraduate student advisor in selecting a project and a supervisor.

ENVE.title: Architecture and the Environment
ENVE.description: Impacts of the environment on architecture; deterioration, freeze/thaw, solar heat, air pollution,  moisture; Impacts of architecture on the environment; ecologic footprint, energy consumption, air quality, waste generation; designing with the environment; renewable energy, effective siting and landscape, passive solar energy, natural lighting, energy efficiency.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one and a half hours a week

ENVE.title: Process Analysis for Environmental Engineering
ENVE.description: Material and energy balances for reacting and non-reacting systems. Applications in mining, metallurgy, pulp and paper, power generation, energy utilization. Emissions to the environment per unit product or service generated. Introduction to life cycle analysis, comparative products and processes.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures two hours a week, problem analysis three hours a week

ENVE.title: Microbiology
ENVE.description:
The biology of the Bacteria, Archaea, Viruses and Protozoans, from the fundamentals of cell chemistry, molecular biology, structure and function, to their involvement in ecological and industrial processes and human disease.
Also listed as BIOL 2303.

ENVE.title: Water Treatment Principles and Design
ENVE.description: Theoretical aspects of unit operations for water treatment with design applications. Topics include water characteristics and contaminants, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, adsorption, ion exchange, membrane processes, disinfection and disinfection by-products, and management of water treatment residuals. Laboratory procedures: settling operations, filtration, aeration, and adsorption.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week, laboratory three hours alternate weeks

ENVE.title: Environmental Engineering Systems Modeling
ENVE.description: Engineered systems for pollution abatement; chemical reaction engineering; reaction kinetics and rate data analysis; design and modeling of reactors; single and multiple reactions; ideal and nonideal reactors; single and multi-parameter models; biochemical reaction engineering; process control. Laboratory procedures: reactor systems performance: Batch, CSTR and PFR.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis 2 hours a week, laboratory 1

ENVE.title: Water Resources Engineering
ENVE.description:
A quantitative analysis of natural water systems and the development of these systems as a resource. Components of the hydrologic cycle. Quantitative analysis of stream flow. Probability concepts in water resources. Reservoir design and operation. Hydraulic properties and availability  of groundwater. Storm water management.
Also listed as GEOG 4103.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week

ENVE.title: Contaminant and Pollutant Transport in the Environment
ENVE.description: Physical phenomenon governing the transport of contaminants in the environment: diffusion, advection, dispersion, sorption, interphase transfer. Derivation and application of transport equations in air, surface and groundwater pollution; analytical and numerical solutions. Equilibrium partitioning of contaminants among air, water, sediment, and biota.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week

ENVE.title: Environmental Geotechnical Engineering
ENVE.description: Landfill design; hydrogeologic principles, water budget, landfill liners, geosynthetics, landfill covers, quality control/quality assurance, clay leachate interaction, composite liner design and leak detection. Landfill operation, maintenance and monitoring. Case studies of landfill design and performance. Geotechnical design of environmental control and containment systems.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week

ENVE.title: Air Pollution and Emissions Control
ENVE.description: Air pollutants, classification, sources, and effects. Ambient air quality objectives and monitoring. Pollutant formation mechanisms in combustion. Major pollutant categories and control methods. Indoor air quality. Laboratory procedures: emissions from boilers and IC engines, particulate size distribution and control, IAQ parameters.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week, laboratory three hours alternate weeks

ENVE.title: Wastewater Treatment Principles and Design
ENVE.description: Theoretical aspects of unit operations and processes for wastewater treatment with design applications. Topics include wastewater characteristics, flow rates, primary treatment, chemical unit processes, biological treatment processes, advanced wastewater treatment, disinfection, biosolids treatment and disposal.  Laboratory procedures: activated sludge, anaerobic growth, chemical precipitation, disinfection.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week, laboratory three hours alternate weeks

ENVE.title: Contaminant Hydrogeology
ENVE.description: Theory of flow through porous media. Site investigation: geology, hydrology and chemistry. Contaminant transport. Unsaturated and multiphase flow. Numerical modeling. Site remediation and remediation technologies.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one and a half hours a week

ENVE.title: Waste Management
ENVE.description: Municipal, hazardous, and mine waste management. Waste composition and potential impacts, collection and transport, recycling and reuse, biological and thermal treatments, isolation. Integrated waste management planning.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one hour a week

ENVE.title: Environmental Planning and Impact Assessment
ENVE.description: Canada and U.S. environmental regulations. Framework for Environmental Impact Assessment, survey techniques for impact assessment and EIA review process. Case studies of selected engineering projects. Environmental planning, management of residuals and environmental standards. Risk assessment, policy development and decision-making. Fault-tree analysis.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis three hours alternate weeks

ENVE.title: Green Building Design
ENVE.description:
Concepts, calculations, modeling; design of green buildings and their components; sustainable sites and landscaping; passive design; building envelope; building materials; daylighting; heating, cooling, and ventilation; building-integrated renewable energy systems; indoor environmental quality; overview of building standards and codes.
Also listed as ACSE 3105.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, problem analysis one and a half hours per week

ENVE.title: Indoor Environmental Quality
ENVE.description:
Indoor environmental quality (air quality, thermal, visual, and acoustic comfort); physical and chemical parameters for characterization. Types and sources of indoor air pollution and discomfort; measurement techniques. Heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting practices and issues. Modelling of and design for indoor environmental quality.
Also listed as ACSE 4106.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, laboratory three hours alternate weeks

ENVE.title: Building Services Engineering
ENVE.description:
This course provides details on how buildings are designed and operated. The materials provide foundational knowledge to understand building services: mechanical, electrical, plumbing systems with associated controls.
Also listed as ACSE 4107.
ENVE.schedule: Lecture three hours per week, problem analysis three hours every other week

ENVE.title: Climate Change and Engineering
ENVE.description: Survey of the physical science of climate change, impacts on the built environment, and climate adaptation in engineering. Greenhouse gases, global warming, paleoclimatology, and Earth system responses. Climate change impacts on structural, water, transportation, and energy systems. Climate vulnerability assessment, examples of design adaptation.
ENVE.schedule: Lecture three hours per week, problem analysis three hours every other week

ENVE.title: Engineering Research Project
ENVE.description: A research project in engineering analysis, design or development carried out by individual students or small teams, for an opportunity to develop initiative, self-reliance, creative ability and engineering judgment and is normally intended for students with high CGPAs and an interest in graduate studies.

ENVE.title: Undergraduate Directed Study
ENVE.description: Student carries out a study, analysis, and solution of an engineering problem which results in a written final report. Carried out under close supervision of a faculty member. Intended for students interested in pursuing graduate studies. Requires supervising faculty member and proposal from student.

ENVE.title: Design Project
ENVE.description: Teams of students develop professional level experience through a design project that incorporates fundamentals acquired in previous mathematics, science, engineering, and complementary studies courses. A final report and oral presentations are required.
ENVE.schedule: Lectures two hours alternate weeks, problem analysis three hours a week

ERTH.title: The Earth and Life Odyssey: A Journey Through Billions of Years
ERTH.description: Embark on a thrilling journey through Earth's epic history! Discover the groundbreaking events and powerful forces that shaped our planet, revealing the dramatic story behind the world we live in today.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, a laboratory three hours per week, and a field excursion

ERTH.title: Earth's Epic Tale: A Story Across Billions of Years
ERTH.description:
Embark on a thrilling journey through Earth's epic history! Discover the groundbreaking events and powerful forces that shaped our planet, revealing the dramatic story behind the world we live in today.
Precludes additional credit for ERTH 1002, ERTH 1006 (no longer offered), ERTH 1009 (no longer offered), ERTH 1010 (no longer offered) and ERTH 1011 (no longer offered).
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Maps, Satellites and the Geospatial Revolution
ERTH.description:
Introduction to the creation and use of maps using a variety of geospatial tools to better understand and resolve physical, social and environmental problems. Overview of geomatics (cartography and map design, geographic information systems, GPS, remote sensing).
Also listed as GEOM 1004.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures and laboratory, four hours a week

ERTH.title: Planet Hollywood
ERTH.description:
Earth Science concepts and content portrayed in Hollywood films are sometimes accurate but more frequently misrepresented. This course will examine popular Hollywood films to critically evaluate the Earth Science concepts and content that they present and directly compare them to the actual science.
Online modules, bi-weekly film screenings and discussions four hours per week.

ERTH.title: Mineralogy to Petrology
ERTH.description: Chemical, optical and crystallographic properties of common rock-forming minerals, with introduction to common mineral assemblages of igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Geodynamics
ERTH.description: The structure, composition, and rheological properties of the Earth: lithosphere, mantle and core. Plate tectonics and its relation to geophysical fields, driving mechanisms, and processes at plate boundaries and in plate interiors.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Geochemistry
ERTH.description: This course looks at geochemical processes from deep Earth to surface environments, and the use of geochemical pathways in order to better understand the Earth’s history.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture 1; laboratory three hours per week

ERTH.title: Paleontology
ERTH.description: Introduction to macrofossil and microfossil groups, their paleoenvironmental significance, and principles of evolutionary paleoecology.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Sedimentation and Stratigraphy
ERTH.description: Origin of sediments and their transport, distribution, and primary structures; processes of sediment-to-rock transformation; spatial patterns; controls of stratigraphy; methods of correlation.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Paleoecology
ERTH.description: Introduction to macrofossil and microfossil groups, their paleoenvironmental significance, and principles of evolutionary paleoecology.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week

ERTH.title: Dinosaurs
ERTH.description: A general introduction to dinosaurs, their place in evolution, their social behaviour, the Mesozoic landscape and extinction theories.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Climate Change: An Earth Sciences Perspective
ERTH.description: An exploration of the often dramatic climate changes that have occurred through earth history from a geological perspective, emphasizing the history of earth climates, geological causes of climate change and impact that rapid climate change has had on the biosphere.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Introduction to Oceanography
ERTH.description: An environmental approach to understanding the oceans; introducing the physical and biological aspects of oceanography, marine resources and marine pollution.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours per week

ERTH.title: Engineering Geoscience
ERTH.description: Applications of the basic concepts of geology, earth materials and earth processes to practical engineering and environmental science. Topics include rock and soil mechanics, slope stability, hydrogeology, geological hazards, and site investigations. Overview of related geophysical methods.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Structural Geology
ERTH.description: Structures and deformation of earth materials.  Topics include stress, strain, folding and faulting.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture three hours a week and a laboratory 3 hours a week

ERTH.title: Natural Disasters
ERTH.description:
Physical characteristics and causes of natural disasters of geological origin such as volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunami, landslides, hurricanes and meteor impacts. Discussion on historical perspective, societal impact and mitigation strategies. Emphasis on Canadian case histories.
Precludes additional credit for ERTH 1003 (no longer offered).
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: On the Origin of Planets
ERTH.description: Origin and evolution of all planetary objects in the solar system. Topics include the geology of comets, asteroids, the terrestrial planets and rocky moons, Earth's formation and early evolution, ocean worlds, the search for exoplanets and detection of extraterrestrial life.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: UNESCO World Geoparks and Geoheritage
ERTH.description: Development of the geologic sciences and enhanced knowledge of the Earth and its history through the lens of inspiring and extraordinary global geological sites that have contributed significantly to science and culture.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: A Geologic Tour of the National Parks of North America
ERTH.description: An introduction to the geology of North America's National parks, the ultimate awe-inspiring educational experience, and how these parks collectively tell the story of the processes that have shaped the continent.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Drivers of Climate Change through Geological Time
ERTH.description: A survey of Earth's 4.5-billion-year climate history, focusing on the use of geologic data to understand the drivers of climate change and their impact on the development of the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. Course includes experiential learning assignments.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture three hours per week; also includes additional online synchronous/asynchronous experiential learning practicum

ERTH.title: Field Geology I
ERTH.description: Field analysis using geological, geophysical and computational methods leading to the interpretation of the origins of geological features and processes.

ERTH.title: Igneous Petrology
ERTH.description: Origins and evolution of igneous rocks through partial melting, crystallization, degassing, and assimilation of host rocks.  Phase diagrams and classification schemes will be used to provide systematic tools for the description and interpretation of igneous rocks.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture three hours per week, a laboratory three hours per week

ERTH.title: Vertebrate Evolution: Mammals, Reptiles, and Birds
ERTH.description: Evolution of mammals, reptiles and birds.  Emphasis on surveying amniote diversity, and the origin of key amniote transformations, as evidenced by the fossil record.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Vertebrate Evolution: Fish and Amphibians
ERTH.description: Evolution of fish and amphibians.  Emphasis on surveying fish and amphibian diversity, and the origin of key transformations of these groups, as evidenced by the fossil record.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Geology of Human Origins
ERTH.description: The origin and evolution of our species from geological, biological and cultural perspectives. The course traces human ancestry from our primate roots through time and changing environments, and explores controversies, frauds, and misperceptions.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours per week

ERTH.title: Evolution of Mammals, Reptiles and Birds
ERTH.description:
Evolution of mammals, reptiles and birds. Emphasis on surveying amniote diversity, and the origin of key amniote transformations, as evidences by the fossil record.
Precludes additional credit for ERTH 3111 and BIOL 3111.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours per week

ERTH.title: Evolution of Fish and Amphibians
ERTH.description:
Evolution of fish and amphibians. Emphasis on surveying fish and amphibian diversity and the origin of key transformations of these groups, as evidenced by the fossil record.
Precludes additional credit for ERTH 3112 and BIOL 3112.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours per week

ERTH.title: Mineral Deposits
ERTH.description: Analysis and interpretation of the geological and geochemical processes responsible for mineral deposit genesis in a global context.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Physical Hydrogeology
ERTH.description: Principles of deep- to shallow fluid flow within the Earth's crust, and introduction to the exploration, development and management of groundwater as a global resource.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture three hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Metamorphic Petrology and Processes
ERTH.description: Genesis of metamorphic rocks as determined from field, petrographic and geochemical data.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures two hours a week, a laboratory three hours a week and a field excursion

ERTH.title: Geophysical Methods
ERTH.description: An introduction to the tools of applied geophysics including seismology, electrical, magnetic, and gravitational surveying methods.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Isotope Geochemistry and Geochronology
ERTH.description: This course looks at stable and radiogenic isotope systematics applied to different Earth environments. Students will delve into geochronological techniques and their applications, and apply the principles of elemental and isotopic fractionation to investigate several geological processes.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture 1; laboratory three hours per week

ERTH.title: Directed Studies in Earth Sciences
ERTH.description: One or more projects involving at least 15 days field and/or laboratory research, not related to thesis research. Assessment based on written reports and an oral presentation. Expenses for long-distance travel are borne by the student.

ERTH.title: Special Topics in Earth Sciences
ERTH.description: Field, laboratory or literature research, not related to thesis research. Assessment based on written reports and an oral presentation. Expenses for travel are borne by the student.

ERTH.title: Field Environmental Geobiology
ERTH.description: Exploration of the relationship between micro- and macro-ecological and evolutionary processes and the Earth's physical and chemical environment. Paleobiology and evolutionary ecology in the context of paleoceanography, paleolimnology and/or paleoclimatology. Will include one or two weeks of field based instruction with costs borne by student.

ERTH.title: Evolutionary Developmental Paleobiology
ERTH.description: This course explores the mechanistic basis of organismic evolution from genetic, morphogenetic and epigenetic perspectives, within a phylogenetic context of living and extinct vertebrates.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures or seminars three hours per week

ERTH.title: Topics in Paleobiology and Evolution
ERTH.description: This multidisciplinary seminar course investigates various topics in paleobiology, paleoecology and evolutionary theory.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures and seminar discussion, three hours per week

ERTH.title: Geotechnical Mechanics
ERTH.description: Soil composition and soil classification. Soil properties, compaction, seepage and permeability. Concepts of pore water pressure, capillary pressure and hydraulic head. Principle of effective stress, stress-deformation and strength characteristics of soils, consolidation, stress distribution with soils, and settlement. Laboratory testing.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week, laboratory three hours alternate weeks

ERTH.title: Contaminant and Remediation Hydrogeology
ERTH.description: Geochemical and physical processes controlling contaminant release, migration, and fate in groundwater along with the processes and techniques used for contaminant mitigation and remediation. Examples will include organic and inorganic contaminants in a variety of settings.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours per week and a laboratory three hours per week

ERTH.title: Mineral Exploration Field Geology
ERTH.description: Introduction to the essentials of conducting geological mapping campaign in the Canadian Shield in a field area that has seen considerable industry exploration for volcanogenic massive sulfide mineralization. Activities include outcrop and trench mapping, strain analysis, interpretation of geophysical data, drilling proposals, report writing.

ERTH.title: Frozen Earth: Unveiling the Snowball Earth Catastrophe
ERTH.description: Discover how icy cataclysms shaped our planet through Earth’s most extreme climate event: Snowball Earth! We will explore this theory's origins, examine compelling geologic and geochemical evidence, and dive into topics such as glacial sedimentology, the carbon cycle, evolution, and more on this thrilling adventure.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours per week

ERTH.title: Advanced Sedimentary Geology and Earth History
ERTH.description: The origin, composition and diagenesis of sedimentary rocks throughout Earth history. Study of modern and ancient sedimentary  systems; development of facies models; petrographic and geochemical analysis of sedimentary rocks.
ERTH.schedule: Lecture two hours a week and a laboratory three hours a week

ERTH.title: Advanced Petrology
ERTH.description: Analysis of the physical and chemical conditions, rock-forming processes, as well as the tectonic settings, that control the formation of different rock types. May include one to two weeks of field-based instruction, with costs borne by the student.
ERTH.schedule: lectures or seminars three hours per week

ERTH.title: Physics of the Earth
ERTH.description: The physical properties of the solid Earth. Gravitational, magnetic and palaeomagnetic fields; seismology and earthquake occurrence; heat flow and thermal history. Geodynamic processes.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Field Geology II
ERTH.description: Field camp integrating advanced field, theory and experimental data. Assessment is based on reports, seminars, and oral examinations. Part of the cost is borne by the student. Departmental funding assistance is available for only one 4000-level field course per student.

ERTH.title: Vertebrate Paleontology Field Camp
ERTH.description: Field camp extends the student's vertebrate paleontological knowledge by integrating field, theory, and experimental data. Assessment based on written reports and seminars. Part of the cost is borne by the student. Departmental funding assistance is available for only one 4000-level field course per student.

ERTH.title: Natural Hazards in Canada
ERTH.description: Overview of the main natural hazards (such as floods, landslides, forest fires, earthquakes) and severe weather phenomena (such as ice storms, hail, tornadoes) in the Canadian environment. Risk of catastrophic events and their impact on society and infrastructure.
ERTH.schedule: Lectures three hours a week

ERTH.title: Honours Thesis
ERTH.description: Independent studies. Requires prior written approval of a topic from a supervisor and the course co-ordinator. Oral and written proposal, progress and defence reports are required.

ERTH.title: Research in Earth Sciences
ERTH.description: Understanding research methods, data interpretation and presentation, through readings, seminars and-or laboratory projects related to a topic selected by the student with approval of a faculty advisor.

ESLA.title: Introductory English as a Second Language for Academic Purposes
ESLA.description: For students with little or no experience with academic English. Introduction to integrated language strategies, critical thinking, and basic research techniques for success at university. Attendance and participation are compulsory.

ESLA.title: Intermediate English as a Second Language for Academic Purposes
ESLA.description: For students with moderate experience with academic English. Development and application of academic language conventions, critical thinking and research strategies for success at university. Attendance and participation are compulsory.

ESLA.title: Advanced English as a Second Language for Academic Purposes
ESLA.description: For students needing further refinement of academic English. Analysis and synthesis of academic texts and consolidation of academic language and research practices. Attendance and participation are compulsory.

ESLA.title: English Language Development for Specific Purposes I
ESLA.description: For students in designated programs. Designed primarily for students whose first language is not English. Topics to be determined.

ESLA.title: English Language Development for Specific Purposes II
ESLA.description: For students in designated programs. Designed primarily for students whose first language is not English. Topics to be determined.

EURR.title: Introduction to European and Russian Studies
EURR.description: An introduction to the study of Europe and Russia, including aspects of the histories, societies, cultures, and politics of the region.

EURR.title: European, Russian and Eurasian Politics, Society and International Affairs
EURR.description:
An interdisciplinary examination of the domestic issues facing the countries of Europe, Russia and Eurasia and the position of these countries in a global context, including geopolitical, economic, security and human dimensions.
Precludes additional credit for EURR 2001 (no longer offered), EURR 2002 (no longer offered).
EURR.schedule: Lecture and discussion three hours a week

EURR.title: Europe, Russia and Eurasia Beyond Borders: Literature and Culture
EURR.description:
An exploration of the cultural borders and boundaries of contemporary Europe, Russia and Eurasia. Using literary and visual texts, the course explores issues such as migration, cultural and political borders and their transcendence, cultural responses to authoritarianism, the Cold War and its afterlives, and memory.
Also listed as ENGL 3020.Precludes additional credit for EURR 3001 (no longer offered), EURR 3002 (no longer offered).
EURR.schedule: Lecture and discussion three hours a week

EURR.title: Post-Soviet States and Societies
EURR.description:
The relationship between social forces and state structures at both the national and local levels in the USSR and the post-Soviet states.
Also listed as PSCI 4502.

EURR.title: Nationalism in Russia and Eurasia
EURR.description: Ethnic basis of nationalism in the region. Ethnic politics and trends.

EURR.title: Nation-Building in Central and Eastern Europe
EURR.description: Processes of nation building in the region examined in terms of a particular country, or set of countries.

EURR.title: The Balkans in Transition – 1918 to 1989
EURR.description:
The seminar uses the concept of transition to understand the Balkan encounter with modernity and Europe. Key periods to be examined include the interwar era and the period of communist rule, with an emphasis on political, social and economic themes.
Also listed as HIST 4605.

EURR.title: The Balkans since 1989
EURR.description:
Selected topics in Balkan politics and society since the collapse of communism in 1989, focusing on the democratic transition and the EU accession process.  The legacies of communist rule, democratization and the many national questions that still exist in the region.
Also listed as PSCI 4507.

EURR.title: The Great Russian Novel
EURR.description:
A study of masterpieces of prose fiction from the Golden Age of Russian literature.  Readings will be chosen from writers such as Turgenev, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Gogol, and/or others.  All texts will be studied in English translation.
Also listed as ENGL 4600.

EURR.title: European Integration and European Security
EURR.description: Issues related to the formation of supra-national decision-making structures in Europe.

EURR.title: Selected Topics in European Integration Studies
EURR.description:
Selected topics related to European integration in the post-World War II period.
Also listed as PSCI 4609.

EURR.title: Russia’s Regional and Global Ambitions
EURR.description: Domestic conditions in Russia from 2000 to the present and the framing of Russia’s foreign policy and strategic objectives towards the former Soviet republics and other key global actors, including the United States, the European Union, NATO and China.

EURR.title: Special Topics in European Studies
EURR.description: A seminar focusing on selected topics related to Europe.

EURR.title: Special Topics in Russian and Eurasian Studies
EURR.description: A seminar focusing on selected topics related to Russia and neighbouring countries.

EURR.title: Central Europe, Past and Present
EURR.description:
Evolution and current status of Central Europe from periods of foreign control in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries to independent statehood, with  emphasis on national accommodations and conflicts.
Also listed as HIST 4604.

EURR.title: Politics of Identity in Europe and the Russian Area
EURR.description: The relationships between political transformation, identity-building, ethnicity, and gender politics in post-communist states, considered in comparison with select countries in Central and/or Western Europe.

EURR.title: Internship and Applied Policy Skills
EURR.description: A seminar accompanying an unpaid internship placement to develop workplace and applied policy skills. Relating applied experience to academic literature. Writing skills for an applied policy setting. Internship placement: 12 days over l2 weeks.

EURR.title: Politics of Central Eurasia
EURR.description: Examination of the Caucasus and Central Asia, from Chechnya to former Soviet republics of the region, Afghanistan and Chinese Turkestan. Interests of Russia, China, and the United States. Emphasis on underdevelopment, oil and gas, terrorism, Islam.

EURR.title: Foreign Policies of Soviet Successor States
EURR.description:
The foreign policies of the USSR and of Russia and selected other successor states, with special emphasis on the search for a new security order.
Also listed as PSCI 4601.

EURR.title: Politics of the Caucasus and Caspian Basin
EURR.description: Examination of the South Caucasus (Azerbaijan, Georgia, Armenia), the Russian-held North Caucasus, including Chechnya, and relations with Iran. Emphasis on state and society, oil and gas, transregional communications, interests of western powers, ethnic relations.

EURR.title: EU Summer Study Abroad
EURR.description: This course is open only to students in approved summer study options in Europe, particularly the EU Study Tour.

EURR.title: Contemporary Europe: From Postwar to the European Union
EURR.description: History of contemporary Europe from 1945 to present covering both eastern and western halves of the continent and including social, cultural, political, and economic dimensions.

EURR.title: Europe and International Migration
EURR.description: Europe’s role in international migration. Topics to be discussed may include migration and mobility as both assets and challenges for sending, transit, and destination countries, changing geographies of migration, inclusion and exclusion, political mobilization, and responses of European states and other actors.

EURR.title: Imperial Russia and the Russian Revolution
EURR.description: Examination of the expansion and downfall of tsarist Russia from the eighteenth century to the revolutionary era and the establishment of Bolshevik rule.  Topics include the relationship between the monarchy and subject peoples, social and economic change, and daily life.

EURR.title: The Soviet Union: Power and Culture
EURR.description: Examination of the rise of the Soviet Union to a global power and subsequent tensions that promoted its collapse.  The course will analyze Stalinism, the Second World War, the Thaw, and Brezhnev and Gorbachev eras through the lens of the USSR’s citizens.

EURR.title: The Business Environment in Europe
EURR.description:
The economic, political, legal, and cultural environment for doing business in the European Union and other regions in Europe. Patterns of foreign trade and investment, market characteristics, science and technology, regulation and European integration, and business culture.
Also listed as BUSI 4704.Precludes additional credit for EURR 4006 (no longer offered), BUSI 4604 (no longer offered).

EURR.title: Tutorial in European and Russian Studies
EURR.description: Tutorials or reading courses on selected topics may be arranged with the permission of the Institute and agreement of the instructor.

EURR.title: Honours Essay
EURR.description: Individual research project resulting in a major essay, completed under the supervision of a faculty member and evaluated by the supervisor and a second reader. Students should consult with the Supervisor of Undergraduate Studies regarding the topic and supervisor. Institute’s Honours Essay guidelines apply.

FILM.title: Introduction to Film Studies
FILM.description: Introduction to the study of film that emphasizes problems and methods of film analysis through the study of various types of films. Topics relating to the filmmaker, film genre, and film history are covered through a focus on questions of style and technique.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, discussion one hour a week

FILM.title: Seminar in Film Studies
FILM.description:
A seminar in the study of film that emphasizes problems and methods of film analysis through the study of a variety of types of films.
Precludes additional credit for FILM 1101, FILM 1000 (no longer offered) and FYSM 1510.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, discussion one hour a week

FILM.title: Film Theory and Analysis I
FILM.description:
Introduction to major film theories and analytical practices. The objective of this course is to familiarize students with the main theories and methods of analysis that have been developed for the study of film.
Precludes additional credit for FILM 2000 (no longer offered).
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, seminar one hour a week

FILM.title: Film Theory and Analysis II
FILM.description:
Building on the skills acquired in FILM 2001, this course considers specific debates in film theory, and provides students with advanced methods for film analysis.
Precludes additional credit for FILM 2000 (no longer offered).
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, seminar one hour a week

FILM.title: The Film Industry
FILM.description: The organization of the production, distribution and exhibition practices of various film industries. May include an examination of the relationship between a national film industry and its television industry.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: The Documentary
FILM.description:
An examination of the work of individual filmmakers, of documentary styles and of organizations and institutions in the context of the history of documentary film making, including documentaries made for television. Non-fiction films other than documentaries may be considered.
Also listed as JOUR 2106.Precludes additional credit for FILM 2105 (no longer offered), JOUR 2105 (no longer offered).
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: National Cinema
FILM.description: This course examines the film production of specific countries in order to determine the themes, the styles, and the character of a national cinema.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: Japanese Cinema
FILM.description: Various practices and movements in the history of Japanese cinema, ranging from the silent era to the current digital age.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: Scandinavian Cinema
FILM.description: The development of cinema culture and film production in the Scandinavian countries, from the golden age of Scandinavian silent cinema to contemporary Nordic noir.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: Indigenous Cinema and Media
FILM.description: A critical examination of films and other audiovisual media created by Indigenous artists, such as independent films, genre films, documentaries, web series, installations, and video games.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: Canadian Cinema
FILM.description:
A critical examination of Canadian cinema and media and how it relates to other aspects of Canadian culture.
Precludes additional credit for FILM 2207 (no longer offered), FILM 2208 (no longer offered), FILM 2209 (no longer offered).
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, seminar one hour a week

FILM.title: Authorship in Film and Media
FILM.description: A detailed study of the themes, the characteristic style, development and influence of one or more directors.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: Film Genres
FILM.description: This course examines questions of generic form, drawing examples from world cinema.
FILM.schedule: Lecture and screening three hours a week, lecture one hour a week

FILM.title: History of World Cinema I
FILM.description:
Historical survey of world cinema primarily from 1895 to 1945, examining the forms, structures and stylistic conventions of various periods and nations.
